Dimonah
dih-MOH-nah
proper noun
Hebrew Dimonah, perhaps “dunghill” or “place of silence,” a town in the south of Judah.

Biblical Definition

Dimonah was a town in the uttermost south of Judah, named in the catalogue of the cities of that tribe toward the coast of Edom (Jos 15:22). It lay among the towns of the dry Negeb, on the thirsty frontier where the LORD settled His people and proved them by the hardness of the land. Some take it to be the same place as Dibon, named among the villages of Judah re-inhabited after the captivity (Neh 11:25), for the southern names are sometimes written with small variation in the records of Scripture. Dimonah is one of the obscure towns of the southland that left no further mark in the sacred history, yet it was written into the word of God among the inheritance of Judah, near the head of the southern list, hard by Kabzeel the southernmost town. The dry south was a place of testing, where Israel learned that life came not from a well-watered country but from the provision of the LORD; and into that hard land the covenant people were planted by lot. Dimonah stands as a witness that the God who divided the land remembered even the least of its towns, recording their names in His word, that the faithfulness of His allotment to the tribes of His covenant might never be forgotten.

Webster 1828 Definition

A town in the uttermost south of Judah, perhaps the same as Dibon, in the dry Negeb.

DIMONAH, a town in the uttermost south of Judah (Jos 15:22).

It lay in the dry Negeb toward the coast of Edom.

Some take it to be the same as Dibon (Neh 11:25).

It stood near the head of the southern list of towns.

It was written into Scripture among Judah’s inheritance.

Key Scripture

Jos 15:22 — "And Kinah, and Dimonah, and Adadah,"

Jos 15:21 — "And the uttermost cities of the tribe of the children of Judah toward the coast of Edom southward were Kabzeel, and Eder, and Jagur,"

Neh 11:25 — "And for the villages, with their fields, some of the children of Judah dwelt at Kirjath-arba, and in the villages thereof, and at Dibon, and in the villages thereof, and at Jekabzeel, and in the villages thereof,"

Jos 15:1 — "This then was the lot of the tribe of the children of Judah by their families; even to the border of Edom the wilderness of Zin southward was the uttermost part of the south coast."

Modern Corruption

A place of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses that God remembered even the least of the towns He divided by lot.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the God who divided the land remembered even the least of its towns. Dimonah was an obscure village of the dry south that left no further mark in the sacred history, yet the LORD wrote it into His word among the inheritance of Judah. The dry south was a place of testing, where Israel learned that life came not from a well-watered country but from the provision of God; and into that hard land the covenant people were planted by lot, none of them forgotten by Him.

The recording of so small a town near the head of the southern list, hard by Kabzeel the southernmost, witnesses the care of God in the allotment of His people’s heritage. He knew their borders to the last village, and set down their names that His faithfulness might be known to every generation. The LORD does not number His towns by their fame; He remembered Dimonah as truly as the great cities, that the praise of His covenant-keeping might rise even from the obscure frontier of the Negeb.

Hebrew Roots

The name perhaps means “dunghill” or “place of silence,” borne by an obscure town of the south.

Dimonah — Hebrew Dimonah, perhaps “place of silence.”

It lay in the uttermost south of Judah, in the Negeb.

It stood near Kinah and Adadah on the frontier.

Some take it to be the same as Dibon.

It was written into Scripture among Judah’s inheritance.

Usage

"Like Dimonah, the God who divided the land remembered even the least of its towns."

"Dimonah teaches that the LORD does not number His towns by their fame but keeps them all."

"Its obscurity shows that the praise of God’s covenant rises even from the frontier of the Negeb."
